articles.sourceTitle: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks
articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours'
articles.text:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

Updated with response from Barracuda.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

articles.sourceTitle: Generative AI Usage in the Games Industry
articles.title: On Generative AI Usage in the Games Industry
articles.text:
The following manifesto was written by members of the IWGB Game Workers' Branch in collaboration with members of Game Workers Unite Ireland of the Republic of Ireland, CSVI of Spain, and the FIOM-CGIL Milan Work Council

Impact
Recommendations
Conclusion
FAQ
References

Introduction
Our Aims
We, a collective of video game unions and work councils from Europe, write this manifesto to raise awareness of the harms of generative AI (genAI) use within the video game development sector.
GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce. Left unchecked, this harm will continue to grow and impact more workers, more games, and more players, even more acutely.
Our goal is to bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce, as well as to set guidelines and standards for games industry workers, stakeholders, and regulators, suggesting actions which can be taken to reduce – and ideally eliminate – these dangers.
Scope
This manifesto discusses genAI in the context of the video game development sector. These uses include, but are not limited to:

The creation of assets included in a released game which are experienced by players – for example: art, sound, code, and dialogue assets.
The creation of materials which are used as part of the process of development but which players won’t experience when playing the released game – for example: early concept art, reference materials, pre-translations, etc.

By “genAI” we mean a specific type of AI used to generate text, pictures, videos, or music in response to limited inputs (usually just text “prompts”) using LLMs and other energy-intensive models. The wider harms of genAI won't be covered here, but they constitute additional extremely compelling reasons to resist the use of genAI. These include:

Severe harm to the environment (Zewe, 2025)
The destruction of communities (Nguyen, 2025)
The exploitation of the Global South (F.Regilme, 2025)

This document won’t go into detail about how different genAI models work, nor discuss the comparative quality of their output.
The focus of this document is on games industry workers (us!), how we are and will be impacted, and how we can resist.
The Impact of GenAI
GenAI Creates Worse Working Conditions

GenAI is both directly and indirectly replacing game industry workers.
Many game workers are being forced to use genAI, either explicitly or implicitly.
Working with genAI is less desirable, fulfilling, and educational than the same work without genAI.
Over time, working with genAI leads to worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout.
Using genAI removes a sense of ownership from workers.
GenAI is causing a marked decline in junior positions within the industry, leading to a lack of new talent.

Proponents of generative AI claim that it is a tool of empowerment for workers. For that to be true, every worker would be free to choose if, when, and how to use it. We would also need to trust that every employer would use the promised productivity improvements to benefit their workers.
In practice, this is not what we are seeing.
In many workplaces today, workers are being forced to use genAI ‘tools’, sometimes in very specific ways (Plunkett, 2025). Some companies do not explicitly impose the usage of genAI, but set expectations which cannot be reached with or without its use. Allowing the choice of usage, while also creating expectations that the worker should be able to keep pace with automated procedures, is no choice at all (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025).
When workers do use genAI, they find work more onerous than before. Many of the tasks related to genAI work are more tedious and less fulfilling, since the work becomes less about exercising the skills workers have built and invested in, and instead pivots to a plethora of small, parallel tasks which amount to supervising genAI and bug-fixing its output.
Workers using genAI have reported ‘AI brain fry’ and reduced focus (Pearl et al., 2025). Although gains to productivity are possible, these tend to be short term. Employees often initially work faster, take on larger tasks, work overtime, and ignore breaks, due to working with genAI feeling 'more like chatting' (Rangantathan & Ye, 2026). However, once this novelty declines, so does productivity, with workers reporting cognitive fatigue, burnout, and inhibited decision making.
A recent study (Shaw & Nave, 2026) showed that participants who used genAI frequently adopted results that were systematically incorrect, especially under time pressure but also in the face of incentives and feedback. The researchers were able to prove that users of genAI habitually delegate their agency and offload decision making to an external party with relative ease. They call this process ‘cognitive surrender’ (Shaw & Nave, 2026).
The use of genAI also removes a sense of ownership from workers, who become alienated from the results of their labour: the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers’ stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them.
GenAI is disproportionately used for work which would traditionally be given to junior workers, and is hence directly reducing the amount of junior positions available within the industry. This is worsening an already existing problem for newcomers to the industry, who are finding it harder than ever to find work, but it is also a loss of potential fresh perspectives, and is staggeringly short-sighted when it comes to the industry’s sustainable future.
GenAI has a profound negative impact on workers by reducing the availability and appeal of work. Games are best made by people, and people do their best when they are healthy and connected to their work, refining their skills and accumulating real experience.
GenAI Harms Relations Between Workers and Employers

GenAI is sold to employers as an alternative to workers.
GenAI often increases pressure on workers when used by employers to set policy, timescales, etc.
GenAI can be used by employers to abdicate responsibility.

GenAI’s promise to employers is to more fully automate processes, to enable them to be completed with fewer workers. This directly reduces the amount of jobs available for game workers. In some cases, workers have even been forced to train the models which then replaced them, leaving them unemployed.
GenAI interfaces are engineered to be human-like and eager-to-please, to prioritise keeping the user engaged, even if engagement comes at the cost of providing them with incorrect information. GenAI’s predisposition towards this sycophancy and lack of real-world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions (Cheng et al., 2026).
In addition, when employers engage with human-like genAI models which never tell them ‘no’, they become less receptive to criticism and pushback from other workers.
GenAI can also obfuscate and confuse employers’ accountability, in two main ways. Firstly, employers may shift their own accountability onto these platforms, blaming an error on the “tool”, rather than accepting responsibility themselves. Secondly, they may blame workers for issues which arise through the use of genAI – which the employers have mandated.
Any time genAI is used without exacting human verification, the possibility of error increases. Exacting human verification takes time, which negates the promise of genAI automation, and therefore many employers are choosing to skip this step, either directly or indirectly by imposing time constraints on workers which make detailed verification impossible. Workers are then blamed for failures in the genAI’s output.
Employers see genAI as a way of cutting labour costs, employing fewer workers than they would need to without it. GenAI companies ingratiate themselves with employers, by promising the impossible. Moreover, mistakes made by genAI are often blamed on the workers, rather than the employers mandating its use.
GenAI Appropriates the Work of Workers

GenAI models are often trained on stolen third-party data, with employers failing to credit or compensate the original creators.
Where genAI models are trained on internal data, employees/creators are likewise rarely credited or compensated.

GenAI models are mostly trained on stolen datasets, and, as stated by the owner of a genAI company, ‘impossible to create’ without stealing data (Milmo, 2024). Employers often feel entitled to automatically include their employees’ contribution into their internal dataset without consent and/or extra compensation.
This point does not require much explanation, but please do not let the relative smallness of this section undermine its importance: stealing the creations of others is wrong, creating very similar versions of those creations is wrong, and using those similar versions to generate wealth which the original creator does not share in is wrong.
GenAI does not create, it appropriates. Content output by genAI has its origins in the work of humans, who are rarely compensated for that output.
GenAI Perpetuates Discrimination

Most genAI models are trained on datasets that carry an intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities.
GenAI content averages out data used to train the AI, leading to a homogenisation of culture.

GenAI models are trained on vast swathes of historical data which is often unvetted and without context, as they aggregate large amounts of data and look for commonalities to generate a response without any direct connection to reality. The use of old data can reflect outdated opinions and values which we would be horrified at today, as well as generate middle of the road solutions.
The predominance and absence of certain types of people in historical data can also reinforce their predominance or absence in the output of genAI models today: for example, the predominance of white male doctors in historical medical literature may lead genAI models to assume that a referenced doctor is white, or to create a white male character when asked to create a doctor.
Within the games industry, this has two main types of effect: it can increase discrimination within workplaces, for example, when used in hiring practices, and it can reduce the range of representation within created media, leading to more homogenous characters and viewpoints in the games we create and play.
GenAI reproduces both historical and contemporary biases and can lead to both implicit and explicit discrimination, including but not limited to racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, etc.
GenAI Has Hidden Costs

GenAI’s output is unreliable and often incorrect.
GenAI providers obfuscate the cost of genAI, its inner workings, and its limitations.
GenAI providers aim to silo and monopolise knowledge to sell it back to corporations.

GenAI providers obscure a significant portion of their associated costs (to the environment, mental health, etc.), which impacts the ability of workers to make an informed choice on whether and how to use them (Nguyen, 2025).
GenAI platforms also disincentivise education on their limitations. Average usage of genAI goes down with increased understanding of how genAI actually works behind the scenes (Tully et al., 2025, 20).
GenAI providers sell employers a seductive image of the future, where production can be fully automated. However, in actuality, genAI platforms are gatekeeping transferable skills (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025). Once a model is trained, the ‘owner’ (usually a large conglomerate) of the trained AI has a uniquely powerful position and complete ownership over skills that were previously owned and shared by workers.
This is bad for workers, but it is also bad for employers who outsource their knowledge and skills to third-party genAI providers, as once these comp

"Who is Hiring?" postings stuck near 12-year lows as AI reaches half of all jobs
articles.title: "Who is Hiring?" postings stuck near 12-year lows as AI reaches half of all jobs (November 2026)
articles.text:
November Highlights
Saturday, November 14, 2026

It's been two and a half years since the last update, so this one covers a lot of ground.
As of November 14, November's thread has 244 job postings,
down 37% from 387 at the same point last year. Every thread since July has landed between 224 and 255 postings,
and August's 224 was the fewest since January 2014. So far 2026 averages 287 postings a month,
the lowest yearly average since 2013.

At the same time, AI is now mentioned in more than half of all postings (51.6%), up from 30% two years ago.

AI is in half of all postings

AI appears in 51.6% of November's postings, second only to Remote.
It crossed 50% for the first time in June 2026. Two years ago it was 30%.

The work itself is shifting toward agents. AI agents
(including "agentic") appear in 14.8% of postings, ahead of LLMs at 10.7%.
MCP barely existed a year ago (0.3%) and is now in 4.5% of postings,
the biggest climb in this month's rankings. Meanwhile, the older machine learning
label slipped from 14.8% to 11.5%.

Compare AI, AI Agents, LLM, and Machine Learning

Front-end roles keep shrinking

Figures in this section are three-month averages, which smooth out month-to-month swings,
so they differ a little from the November-only numbers in the chart and tables.
Front End has had the steepest fall of any role label:
from 27% of postings in early 2022 to 6.6% now, and from 15.6% a year ago.
Full Stack (26.2% to 20.1%) and Back End (23.6% to 18.8%)
also dropped over the past year, most of it in the last few months.

Seniority mix has been steadier. Senior has stayed around 30% for years,
Staff has roughly quadrupled since 2019 to about 12%, and
Junior remains rare at around 3%.

Compare Full Stack, Back End, and Front End

Changes to the data

New terms this month: AI Agents, LLM, MCP, RAG, LangChain, Anthropic, pgvector, Vector Database, Bun and Deno.
Every thread back to 2011 is re-analyzed on each run, so their full history is included.

I also fixed a bug where a few terms with alternate spellings didn't count their own name
(for example, "Next.js" was only counted when written "NextJS"). Next.js, NestJS, WebAssembly,
Front End and Back End are higher across all months than in earlier posts.
The December 2011 thread, which has a single posting, is no longer included.

Rankings and movers

articles.sourceTitle: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
articles.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
articles.text: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery.But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will coverdifferent positional methods in LLMs;(finally) how RoPE works;what methods are used by recent open LLMs.Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures.Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here, which also has a navigation bar on the left side.Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.)A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:“The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”“The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps.For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence.(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub.)Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information.The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.Figure 5: GPT-2 adds absolute position information before the transformer blocks, as highlighted in purple. The dimensions shown are for GPT-2 XL.The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and xm the token ID at that position. The input to the first block isHere,Etoken is the embedding layer,Pm is the position info vector selected by m,and hm is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.Figure 6: Token and position embeddings are added element-wise. (I am following the convention here that neural network diagrams are usually read from bottom to top.)In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3]. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding Pm depends on the token’s own position m. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P2 and P7, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)Figure 7: Sinusoidal position encodings added to the token embeddings as highlighted in purple.The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √(dmodel) before adding the position vectors, where dmodel is the embedding width.So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formulathe formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is:This scaling by √(dmodel) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical magnitudes at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them. In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same s

articles.sourceTitle: Parents pay $75k for Alpha's AI school. Half of its students missed math target
articles.title: Wealthy parents pay $75,000 for a two-hour AI school day. Half of students missed the math target
articles.text:
Alpha School, the network of AI-driven private schools charging parents up to $75,000 a year, has won backers from Silicon Valley to the Trump administration. Its own data show most of its students aren’t reaching the model’s central promise.
Only 42% of Alpha students met the network’s goal of learning twice as fast in both math and reading, according to internal data first reported by The New York Times. The findings land as Alpha pushes into public schools, where districts are adopting its software in hopes of fitting more learning into less time.
What Alpha promises parents
Alpha has no traditional teachers. It employs what it calls “guides,” whose job, according to the company’s marketing materials, is to “make every student feel valued and motivated.” Guides don’t plan lessons or grade homework, Fortune reported in September.

The core of the pitch is that students will “learn twice as much as their peers in two hours of academics a day” using TimeBack, an app Alpha markets as an AI tutor. Cofounder MacKenzie Price says the app personalizes and accelerates learning for each student, freeing the rest of the school day for workshops on skills such as public speaking and relationship building.
The network has grown fast. A spokesperson told Fortune in September that Alpha had more than 1,200 students. The Times put the figure at about 1,500 across roughly 50 campuses, in line with the expansion plans Alpha announced in August.
That pitch has drawn AI optimists. “I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends Alpha’s New York campus, told Fortune in September.

In September 2025, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured Alpha’s Austin campus and called its model “the most exciting thing I’ve seen in education in a long time.” LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman have both publicly backed Price and Alpha on X. Even the X account of Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder serving more than 11 years in prison for fraud, praised Price.
Where students are falling short
Math is the bigger gap. About half of K-8 students at Alpha’s private campuses missed the goal of learning math twice as fast, and roughly one in five missed their reading targets, according to the Times‘ review of the network’s data.

Students who started behind fared worse. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37% of that group met the network’s 2x growth goal by winter, the Times found.

The two-hour premise is also in question. Guides and parents told Wired that students worked late into the night to meet the school’s goals. One parent of a 13-year-old reading at an 11th-grade level said reaching those goals came with “stress and anxiety.”

Former employees told 404 Media that Alpha’s AI generated faulty lesson plans, which internal documents said sometimes did “more harm than good,” and that the company scraped other online courses without permission.
Alpha’s model is reaching public schools
More than 2,600 public school students in Texas and South Carolina now use Alpha’s platform, according to company documents reviewed by the Times. That is a tougher test: public schools can’t remove struggling students, the Times noted, and they lack the prize incentives Alpha uses at its private campuses.

The Houston Independent School District, the largest in Texas, is piloting the software at two schools. Superintendent Mike Miles told the Times that students spent more time on Alpha’s apps than planned, cutting into other activities. He still wants AI in the district’s toolkit, calling it an important tool for students to be “successful in a different world and workplace.”

Research points to a learning penalty
Alpha’s expansion comes as schools grapple with falling math and reading scores and growing evidence that how students use AI matters as much as whether they use it.
A study of 26,811 secondary students in central China found that homework scores rose 18% after students adopted generative AI tools, while closed-book exam scores fell 20%. The OECD’s latest PISA results found that daily AI users scored lower in science than nonusers, while moderate users performed about the same.

Professors have told Fortune that students who lean on AI summaries struggle with sustained reading. “Today, if you assign that amount of reading, they often don’t know what to do,” Timothy O’Malley, a theology professor at the University of Notre Dame, told Fortune‘s Preston Fore in June.
“It’s not even an inability to critically think,” Jessica Hooten Wilson, a professor of great books and humanities at Pepperdine University, told Fortune. “It’s an inability to read sentences.”
